<title>Notify 4/9: Custos sender — config, sender keys, registration routes, relay client, first trigger</title>
<description>
Phase 4 of the <issue id="b95fcd23-95fa-43f6-86a6-81defb9dda77" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-311/e2e-encrypted-notification-relay-for-self-hosted-custos-apns">MM-311</issue> notification relay — the PDS side. Implementation details: `docs/design-plans/2026-07-17-notification-relay-implementation.md`.

## Scope

* **Config:** `[notifications]` in `common::Config` — `relay: Option<String>` (node id, default None → off, the `[iroh]` posture), `enrollment_code: Option<String>`; env `EZPDS_NOTIFICATIONS_RELAY` / `EZPDS_NOTIFICATIONS_ENROLLMENT_CODE`; validation requires `[iroh] enabled`.
* **Migrations (V052+):** `notification_sender_keys` (kid autoincrement, secret encrypted under master key per the `iroh_identity` scheme, retired_at/revoked_at), `notification_registrations` keyed **(did, device_uuid)** — NOT FK'd to the transient `devices` table (deleted at DID promotion) — and `admin_notification_registrations` keyed by `admin_devices.id`. Sender keys join `SecretFamily` in `db/kek.rs` for `rewrap-master-key`.
* **Routes** (+ bruno, seq 124+): `POST /v1/notifications/register` + `DELETE /v1/notifications/register/{deviceUuid}` + `GET /v1/notifications/sender-keys` via `authenticate_access` (DPoP — auth-seam-check applies); `POST /v1/admin/notifications/register` + `GET /v1/admin/notifications/sender-keys` via `require_admin` signed envelope. Sender-keys responses are the re-pin surface with versioned kids; rotation = publish new alongside old, retire after overlap; revocation = immediate removal from the set.
* **Relay client:** the PDS's first *outbound* iroh leg — `notify_relay_client` module reusing the existing `IrohState` endpoint to dial the configured node id, one stream per RPC, lazy reconnect with backoff. Sends flow through an in-process mpsc worker (fire-and-forget; in-memory queue only — a missed push is a missed banner, the app reconciles from Custos). Enroll-on-first-contact consumes the config claim code.
* **Sending:** `notifications.rs` owns `notify_device(did, payload)` / `notify_admin_devices(payload)`: pad to bucket, HPKE-seal per registration (fan-out, one seal per device), push, delete the registration on `unregistered`.
* **Cleanup:** `purge_account` gains the registrations delete (+ best-effort `dropHandle`); `revoke_admin_device` path cleans the admin row.
* **First trigger:** agent claim pending (the auth.md ceremony awaiting confirmation).

## Acceptance

* Full loopback e2e: pds ↔ notify-relay ↔ wiremock APNs — register, seal, push; the fixture "device" opens the payload with `crypto::open_notification` and verifies sender authenticity.
* Prune-on-410 e2e: relay returns `unregistered` → registration row deleted.
* Rotation semantics tested: retired key still verifies, revoked key vanishes from the published set.
* Feature entirely inert when `[notifications]` unset. `just ci-pds` + bruno parity green.
</description>

<title>E2E-encrypted notification relay for self-hosted Custos (APNs)</title>
<description>
Implement the notification relay designed in [docs/design-plans/2026-07-10-notification-relay.md](<https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/blob/main/docs/design-plans/2026-07-10-notification-relay.md>) (design PR <pull-request id="34230e45-6259-4c9a-b58d-6b135adf84e3" href="https://linear.app/malpercio/review/design-exploration-e2e-encrypted-notification-relay-for-self-hosted-327f880332d1">malpercio-dev/ezpds#207</pull-request>, **merged** — the doc on `main` is the source of truth and incorporates the review hardening: claim-code enrollment authorization for the official relay, versioned sender keys with re-pin/revocation semantics, explicit v1 replay acceptance, unverified-notice rendering for unauthenticated payloads, per-handle APNs topics, serialized-request padding budget, and the post-reboot keychain window).

## Problem

Self-hosted Custos instances need to deliver push notifications to the official iOS apps (Obsign, admin-companion). APNs auth keys are bundle-ID-bound, so self-hosters cannot push directly — a relay is structurally required. The design makes that relay a **blind courier**: trusted for availability only.

## Architecture (see design doc for full detail)

* **Confidentiality:** payloads HPKE-sealed (RFC 9180, DHKEM-P256 + AES-GCM) to a per-device notification key; decrypted on-device by a Notification Service Extension (`mutable-content: 1`). Neither the relay nor Apple sees plaintext.
* **Integrity:** HPKE Auth mode with pinned, versioned per-instance sender keys — the relay cannot forge authenticated content (it can generate detectable junk pushes and replay; v1 accepts duplicates as benign).
* **Metadata minimization:** opaque push handles bound to the instance's iroh node id (no DIDs/handles/raw tokens at the relay), fixed-size padding budgeted against the serialized APNs request, optional content-free ping mode.
* **Transport:** Custos ↔ relay over iroh, new `ezpds/notify/0` ALPN, reusing the persisted node identity (`iroh_identity`) and `iroh_tunnel.rs` patterns; back-channel carries APNs `410 Unregistered` pruning feedback.
* **Sovereignty:** relay is an open-source workspace crate (`crates/notify-relay/`); any instance points at any relay via `[notifications] relay = "<node id>"`. Official relay requires a claim-code enrollment grant; open enrollment is a config option for self-run relays. Caveat: official bundle IDs require the official relay's APNs key.

## Suggested phasing

1. **Relay crate + Custos sender** — `crates/notify-relay/` (claim-code enrollment grants, handle store with per-handle APNs topic, APNs HTTP/2 client, per-node rate limits, serialized-request size validation with 4 KB boundary test) + `[notifications]` config, device notification-key registration route, versioned sender-key set, sealed-send on first trigger (agent claim pending). Loopback iroh e2e tests with mock APNs.
2. **Wallet NSE** — per-device keypair + shared keychain access group, registration in onboarding, decrypt-and-render extension, unverified-notice fallback + in-app diagnostics.
3. **Admin-companion adoption + operator docs** — ops alert triggers, self-relay runbook, metadata-minimizing ping mode.

## Open questions (from the design doc)

* Enrollment grant distribution for the official relay (ceremony mirrors admin-device pairing)
* Replay hardening beyond v1's accept-duplicates posture (per-device counter + durable replay window)
* Delivery receipts over the iroh back-channel (out of scope v1)
* Android/FCM later (envelope is provider-agnostic)

Not yet scheduled into a wave; split into per-phase issues when picked up.
</description>

# Linear Development Workflow

This skill manages the full lifecycle of working on a Linear issue: from picking it up through opening a PR.

## Starting Work on an Issue

When the user indicates they want to work on a Linear issue (e.g., "Let's work on MM-42"):

1. **Parse the issue identifier** from the user's message. The pattern is `MM-` followed by a number.

2. **Fetch the issue details** from Linear using the `get_issue` tool with the parsed identifier. Display a brief summary to the user: title, description (truncated if long), priority, and any existing labels.

3. **Update the issue in Linear:**
   - Set the status to **"In Progress"**
   - Assign it to **"me"** (the authenticated user)

   Use the `save_issue` tool with the issue's `id`, `state: "In Progress"`, and `assignee: "me"`.

4. **Create a git branch from a fresh base** using the issue's suggested branch name:
   - The `get_issue` response includes a `branchName` field — use that as the branch name.
   - **Fetch first, then branch from the remote tip — never from a possibly-stale local HEAD:**
     `git fetch origin main && git checkout -b <branchName> origin/main`
     A stale base silently duplicates work that already merged (hours lost rebuilding an already-shipped backend is the known failure mode).
   - If the branch already exists locally, check it out, then run `git log --oneline <branchName>..origin/main` and surface to the user how far behind the base is.

5. **Verify sibling work is in the base.** If the issue depends on or overlaps sibling issues already marked Done in Linear, confirm their PRs are actually present in the branch base (e.g. `git log --oneline origin/main | grep -i mm-nnn`, or check for the files/routes they added) before concluding any related feature is "missing". **"Linear says Done but the code isn't here" is a hard stop-and-verify signal — it almost always means your base is stale, not that the feature needs building.**

6. **Confirm to the user** what happened: issue assigned, status updated, branch created/checked out (and from which base commit). Then ask what they'd like to tackle first, or summarize the issue so they can dive in.

## Opening a PR (Auto-transition to "In Review")

When the user asks to open a PR, create a pull request, or you detect that a PR is being created for a branch associated with a Linear issue:

1. **Identify the Linear issue** from the current branch name. Linear branch names typically contain the issue identifier (e.g., `malpercio/mm-42-fix-the-thing`). Extract the `MM-XXX` portion.

2. **Create the PR** as the user requests (follow normal PR creation workflow).

3. **After the PR is successfully created**, update the Linear issue:
   - Set the status to **"In Review"**
   - Attach the PR URL as a link on the issue using the `links` field in `save_issue`

   Use `save_issue` with the issue's `id`, `state: "In Review"`, and `links: [{"url": "<pr-url>", "title": "Pull Request"}]`.

4. **Confirm** to the user that the issue has been moved to "In Review" and the PR link has been attached.

## Important Notes

- Always fetch the issue first to confirm it exists and get the full `id` (UUID) needed for updates.
- If the issue is already "In Progress" and assigned, skip those updates and just create the branch.
- If branch creation fails (e.g., uncommitted changes), inform the user and suggest next steps rather than silently failing.
- The PR-to-"In Review" transition should happen automatically whenever a PR is opened during a session where the user started work on a Linear issue. Track the active issue identifier throughout the session.

1	# Notification Relay — Implementation Plan (MM-311)
2	
3	[MM-311](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-311) · implementation leg of
4	[docs/design-plans/2026-07-10-notification-relay.md](2026-07-10-notification-relay.md)
5	(design PR #207, merged — that doc remains the architecture source of truth; this doc pins
6	the implementation details against the codebase and decomposes the work into issues).
7	
8	**Codebase verified: 2026-07-17** (migrations at V051, bruno seq at 123, iroh 1.0.0,
9	workspace 0.5.2).
10	
11	## Refinements to the design doc
12	
13	Three details discovered during codebase verification refine (not reverse) the design:
14	
15	1. **Registrations key on the account DID, not `devices.id`.** The design says the
16	   registration lands in "new columns/table beside `devices`" — but `devices` is a
17	   *transient pre-DID artifact*: rows are deleted inside the DID-promotion transaction
18	   (`routes/create_did.rs`) and the table FKs to `pending_accounts`. A registration FK'd
19	   there would die exactly when the account starts mattering. Wallet notification
20	   registrations therefore key on `(did, device_uuid)` where `device_uuid` is an
21	   app-generated stable identifier, are created **post-promotion** over the OAuth/DPoP
22	   channel (through the `authenticate_access` seam — the auth-seam-check applies), and are
23	   purged in `account_delete::purge_account`'s explicit FK-ordered delete list.
24	   Admin-companion registrations are a separate table keyed by `admin_devices.id`,
25	   cleaned up alongside the revoke tombstone. Pending (pre-DID) accounts get no pushes —
26	   onboarding completes with promotion, and registration is one of the first
27	   post-promotion calls.
28	2. **The ciphersuite is forced to AES-256-GCM.** CryptoKit ships exactly one P-256 HPKE
29	   suite: `HPKE.Ciphersuite.P256_SHA256_AES_GCM_256`. So the wire suite is pinned to
30	   **DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256) + HKDF-SHA256 + AES-256-GCM, mode_auth** — no
31	   negotiation, ever; `v` in the envelope names the whole suite. RFC 9180's appendix has
32	   no test vector for this exact combo (A.3 is AES-128), so golden fixtures are generated
33	   from the Rust implementation, pinned in `crates/crypto/tests/fixtures/`, and
34	   cross-verified against CryptoKit by an on-device XCTest in the wallet phase.
35	3. **The v1 back-channel is the RPC response, not a server-initiated stream.** The relay
36	   calls APNs synchronously inside the push RPC, so `410 Unregistered` (and throttle/size
37	   outcomes) return in the same request/response exchange over the already-open bidi
38	   stream. No relay-initiated streams in v1 — that machinery (delivery receipts) stays
39	   out of scope, as the design already decided.
40	
41	CryptoKit's HPKE API requires **iOS 17**; the apps' deployment target currently rides
42	tauri-cli's default (13.0, nothing overridden in either `tauri.conf.json`). Decision:
43	raise `bundle > iOS > minimumSystemVersion` to `17.0` for both apps in the wallet phase.
44	Both apps are new (no installed base below 17), and a per-target split (NSE at 17, app
45	lower, runtime-gated registration) buys nothing but complexity.
46	
47	## Wire formats
48	
49	### Sealed payload (Custos → device, opaque to relay/Apple)
50	
51	Plaintext (serde_json, camelCase):
52	
53	```json
54	{ "type": "agent_claim_pending", "title": "…", "body": "…", "data": { … }, "pad": "…" }
55	```
56	
57	`pad` is a string of `0x20` bytes sized so the **serialized APNs request** lands exactly
58	on a padding bucket (below). Sealed with HPKE mode_auth:
59	
60	- suite: DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256), HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM
61	- `info = b"ezpds/notify/1"`, `aad = b""` (version binding lives in `info` + envelope `v`)
62	- sender key: the instance's static notification sender keypair named by `kid`
63	- recipient key: the device's notification public key
64	
65	### APNs payload (relay → Apple → device)
66	
67	```json
68	{
69	  "aps": { "alert": { "title": "Custos", "body": "Encrypted notification" },
70	           "mutable-content": 1 },
71	  "ezpds": { "v": 1, "kid": 3, "enc": "<b64url encapsulated key>", "ct": "<b64url ciphertext>" }
72	}
73	```
74	
75	Ping mode (later phase) replaces `aps` with `{ "content-available": 1 }` and omits
76	`ezpds` entirely.
77	
78	### Padding buckets
79	
80	Buckets are defined on the **serialized APNs JSON body**: `{1024, 2048, 3584}` bytes
81	(3584 keeps headroom under APNs' 4096 cap). Base64url expansion is deterministic
82	(`enc` = 65-byte uncompressed P-256 point → 87 chars; `ct` = plaintext + 16-byte tag),
83	so Custos computes the exact `pad` length that makes the final body hit the smallest
84	bucket ≥ the unpadded size, and refuses payloads that exceed the largest bucket. A
85	relay-side check enforces the same cap defensively, with a boundary test at exactly
86	4096 bytes.
87	
88	### Custos ↔ relay RPC (`ezpds/notify/0`)
89	
90	New ALPN beside `ezpds/iroh/0`. One JSON request per bidi stream, response JSON, stream
91	FIN delimits (the `iroh_tunnel.rs` pattern: `read_to_end` with a 64 KiB cap, 30 s
92	per-stream timeout). The dialing node's identity is `connection.remote_id()` — no
93	credential in the messages. Requests are a tagged enum:
94	
95	| request | response | notes |
96	|---|---|---|
97	| `enroll { claimCode? }` | `ok` / `denied` | idempotent; `claimCode` required unless the relay runs open enrollment |
98	| `registerHandle { apnsToken, apnsTopic }` | `{ handle }` | topic must be in the relay's served-topic set; re-registering the same token rotates the handle |
99	| `dropHandle { handle }` | `ok` | idempotent |
100	| `push { handle, kid, enc, ct, priority, ttlSecs, ping }` | `{ outcome }` | outcome ∈ `delivered · unregistered · throttled · tooLarge · notEnrolled · unknownHandle · apnsError` |
101	
102	`unregistered` is the APNs 410 feedback: Custos deletes the registration row on receipt.
103	Every request except `enroll` requires the node id to be enrolled; handles are only ever
104	resolvable by the node id that registered them.
105	
106	The Custos side gains its first **outbound** iroh leg: a `notify_relay_client` module that
107	reuses the existing `IrohState` endpoint (an iroh `Endpoint` both accepts and dials),
108	dials by node id from config, opens one stream per RPC, and reconnects lazily with
109	exponential backoff. Sends are fire-and-forget from callers' perspective: triggers enqueue
110	into an in-process `tokio::sync::mpsc` worker so a dead relay never blocks a request path.
111	v1 queue is in-memory only (a missed push is a missed banner, not lost data — the app
112	reconciles from its Custos); durable queuing is an explicit non-goal.
113	
114	## The relay: `crates/notify-relay/`
115	
116	New workspace member; own binary, own SQLite DB, same stack (tokio + iroh + sqlx +
117	tracing; axum only if/when an HTTP surface appears — v1 has none). Modeled on the pds
118	crate's conventions: pattern comments, `db/` submodules own queries, migrations as
119	`VNNN__*.sql` with the same manifest/runner pattern (copied small, not shared — the
120	runner is ~50 lines and the crates' migration histories are independent).
121	
122	**Schema:**
123	
124	```sql
125	enrollment_codes(code TEXT PK, created_at TEXT NOT NULL, expires_at TEXT NOT NULL,
126	                 consumed_at TEXT, consumed_by_node TEXT)          -- V001
127	enrollments(node_id TEXT PK, enrolled_at TEXT NOT NULL, code_used TEXT)
128	handles(handle TEXT PK,                    -- 128-bit random, base64url
129	        node_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES enrollments(node_id),
130	        apns_token TEXT NOT NULL, apns_topic TEXT NOT NULL,
131	        created_at TEXT NOT NULL, last_push_at TEXT)
132	```
133	
134	Status is derived from timestamps (the `claim_codes` doctrine); enrollment-code redemption
135	is the same atomic guarded-UPDATE shape as `consume_pairing_code`. `(node_id, apns_token)`
136	unique — re-registration rotates the handle in place.
137	
138	**Config** (TOML + env, mirroring `config_loader.rs` posture): iroh secret key path
139	(file-persisted — the relay has no master-key hierarchy; 0600 perms), `open_enrollment: bool`
140	(default false), APNs: `.p8` path, key id, team id, served topics list, endpoint override
141	(`EZPDS_NOTIFY_APNS_URL` — the wiremock seam, same trick as `EZPDS_PLC_DIRECTORY_URL`),
142	sandbox/production toggle. Enrollment codes are minted by a CLI subcommand
143	(`notify-relay mint-code --ttl 60m`) — operator-local, no remote admin surface in v1.
144	
145	**APNs client:** reqwest (workspace 0.13, rustls — ALPN-negotiates h2 against real APNs,
146	h1 against wiremock). Token auth is a hand-rolled ES256 JWT over the existing `p256`
147	dep (header `{alg, kid}` + claims `{iss: team_id, iat}`, base64url, ECDSA-sign — ~30
148	lines; avoids `jsonwebtoken`'s `ring` dependency), cached and refreshed at 50 minutes
149	per Apple's 20–60 min rule. Headers per push: `apns-topic` (from the handle row),
150	`apns-push-type: alert` (or `background` for ping), `apns-priority` (10 alert / 5 ping),
151	`apns-expiration` (now + ttlSecs).
152	
153	**Rate limits:** in-memory token buckets (no persistence — restart forgiveness is fine),
154	two keys: per node id (default 1 000/h, burst 50) and per handle (default 60/h, burst 10);
155	exceeded → `throttled`. Registration RPCs get a per-node bucket too (default 100/h).
156	
157	**Deploy:** a second binary means the root single-binary Dockerfile doesn't cover it; the
158	relay ships its own `crates/notify-relay/Dockerfile` (same builder pattern,
159	`cargo build --release --locked -p notify-relay`) deployed as a Railway service beside
160	pds/mcp-sidecar, Litestream optional (state is re-derivable by re-enrollment — the design
161	already accepts relay state loss). Ops docs in the final phase.
162	
163	## The Custos side (`crates/pds`)
164	
165	**Config:** `[notifications]` in `common::Config` — `relay: Option<String>` (node id;
166	default `None` → feature off, the `[iroh]` posture), `enrollment_code: Option<String>`
167	(consumed on first successful enroll), `ping_mode: bool` (later phase). Env:
168	`EZPDS_NOTIFICATIONS_RELAY`, `EZPDS_NOTIFICATIONS_ENROLLMENT_CODE`. Requires
169	`[iroh] enabled` (validation error otherwise — the endpoint is the dialer).
170	
171	**Migrations (V052+):**
172	
173	```sql
174	notification_sender_keys(kid INTEGER PK AUTOINCREMENT,
175	                         secret_key_encrypted TEXT NOT NULL,   -- AES-GCM under master key, iroh_identity scheme
176	                         created_at TEXT NOT NULL, retired_at TEXT, revoked_at TEXT)
177	notification_registrations(did TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(did),
178	                           device_uuid TEXT NOT NULL,
179	                           notification_public_key TEXT NOT NULL,  -- did:key multibase, validate_device_public_key
180	                           apns_token TEXT NOT NULL, apns_topic TEXT NOT NULL,
181	                           push_handle TEXT,                       -- NULL until relay registration succeeds
182	                           created_at TEXT NOT NULL, updated_at TEXT NOT NULL,
183	                           PRIMARY KEY (did, device_uuid))
184	admin_notification_registrations(admin_device_id TEXT PK REFERENCES admin_devices(id),
185	                                 notification_public_key TEXT NOT NULL,
186	                                 apns_token TEXT NOT NULL, apns_topic TEXT NOT NULL,
187	                                 push_handle TEXT,
188	                                 created_at TEXT NOT NULL, updated_at TEXT NOT NULL)
189	```
190	
191	Sender secret keys are `SecretFamily` variants in `db/kek.rs` so `rewrap-master-key`
192	covers them. Retired = still published for verification, no longer used for sealing;
193	revoked = removed from the published set immediately (the design's compromise path).
194	`purge_account` gains `DELETE FROM notification_registrations WHERE did = ?` (plus a
195	relay `dropHandle` best-effort); `revoke_admin_device` cleanup deletes the admin row
196	the same way.
197	
198	**Routes** (each with a `.bru`, seq 124+):
199	
200	| route | auth | purpose |
201	|---|---|---|
202	| `POST /v1/notifications/register` | `authenticate_access` (DPoP) | body `{deviceUuid, notificationPublicKey, apnsToken, apnsTopic}`; upserts, triggers relay (re-)registration |

In a `.claude/worktrees/*` checkout, `cargo` is **not on PATH** and the worktree has **no `.devenv/`** built — entering its shell (`nix develop`) triggers a cold build (20+ min without the Cachix cache). But the **main checkout** (`/Users/jacob.zweifel/workspace/malpercio-dev/ezpds/.devenv/profile`) is already built, and `rustup` toolchains are user-level (`~/.rustup`, shared).

**So run cargo through the main checkout's devenv, targeting the worktree's manifest:**

```bash
cd /Users/jacob.zweifel/workspace/malpercio-dev/ezpds && \
  nix develop --impure --accept-flake-config -c \
  cargo test --manifest-path <WORKTREE>/Cargo.toml -p <crate>
```

`CARGO_HOME`/registry cache come from the main checkout's `.devenv` (just a cache — fine to share); build artifacts land in the **worktree's** `target/`. First compile of a crate's full dep tree is heavy; reruns are incremental and fast.

Gotchas:
- These commands need broad fs + network (crates.io) access → run with the sandbox **disabled** (`dangerouslyDisableSandbox`). The plain `nix develop` also fails under sandbox with `cannot connect to socket at '/nix/var/nix/daemon-socket/socket': Operation not permitted` — same fix. Network git (tangled `knot.malpercio.dev` SSH, GitHub mirror) also needs sandbox off — `knot.malpercio.dev` is not in the sandbox allowlist.
- `cd` resets after each Bash call (the shell prints "Shell cwd was reset to <worktree>"), so prefix every invocation with the `cd /main-checkout &&`.
- `nix develop`'s `enterShell` runs `rustup toolchain install` (fast no-op if present) and prints devenv task lines before your command's output — `tail`/`grep` past them.
- **`--manifest-path` is load-bearing, and subagents get this wrong.** The main checkout is often on a *different branch* than the worktree. A subagent that `cd`s to the main checkout and runs a bare `cargo build -p <crate>` (no `--manifest-path`) silently compiles the **main checkout's branch**, not the worktree — producing a green "1294 tests passed" that has nothing to do with the code under review. Seen twice in one session (an implementor and a bug-fixer both reported false green this way while the worktree crate didn't even compile). **Verify build/test/clippy claims first-hand** with `--manifest-path <WORKTREE>/Cargo.toml`; don't trust subagent build evidence in a worktree. To defeat stale-`target/` false negatives, `touch` the changed source files before `cargo clippy -p <crate> --all-targets ... -- -D warnings` so it re-analyzes them.

-- V058: The Custos side of the blind-courier notification relay.
--
-- Three tables: the instance's own versioned sender keys, and one registration
-- table per app surface (wallet accounts, admin-companion devices).
--
-- `notification_sender_keys` holds the P-256 secret the instance seals with in
-- HPKE mode_auth. Devices pin the *public* half, so a rotation is a two-sided
-- ceremony rather than a swap: publish the new key alongside the old, seal with
-- the newest, and only retire the old once every device has re-pinned. Status is
-- derived from timestamps (the `claim_codes` doctrine):
--
--   retired_at NULL, revoked_at NULL -- active: published and used for sealing
--   retired_at set                   -- retired: still published so payloads
--                                       sealed before the rotation still verify,
--                                       never used to seal anything new
--   revoked_at set                   -- revoked: gone from the published set
--                                       immediately (the compromise path)
--
-- The secret is AES-256-GCM-wrapped under the master KEK exactly like
-- `iroh_identity` (V022), and joins `SecretFamily::ALL` so `rewrap-master-key`
-- covers it.
CREATE TABLE notification_sender_keys (
    kid                  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    secret_key_encrypted TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at           TEXT NOT NULL,
    retired_at           TEXT,
    revoked_at           TEXT
);

-- `notification_registrations` deliberately does NOT reference `devices`.
-- `devices` is a transient pre-DID artifact: its rows are deleted inside the
-- DID-promotion transaction (`routes/create_did.rs`) and it FKs to
-- `pending_accounts`. A registration anchored there would be destroyed exactly
-- when the account starts mattering. The key is instead (did, device_uuid),
-- where `device_uuid` is an app-generated stable identifier, and registration
-- happens post-promotion over the DPoP-authenticated channel.
--
-- `push_handle` is the relay's opaque per-device handle: NULL until the relay
-- registration round trip succeeds, so a relay that is down at registration time
-- leaves a row we can re-register later rather than losing the device key.
CREATE TABLE notification_registrations (
    did                     TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts (did),
    device_uuid             TEXT NOT NULL,
    notification_public_key TEXT NOT NULL,
    apns_token              TEXT NOT NULL,
    apns_topic              TEXT NOT NULL,
    push_handle             TEXT,
    created_at              TEXT NOT NULL,
    updated_at              TEXT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (did, device_uuid)
) WITHOUT ROWID;

-- The admin-companion analog. Keyed by the admin device itself, because an
-- operator device authenticates as a device (signed envelope), not as an
-- account; the row is cleaned up alongside the revoke tombstone.
CREATE TABLE admin_notification_registrations (
    admin_device_id         TEXT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES admin_devices (id),
    notification_public_key TEXT NOT NULL,
    apns_token              TEXT NOT NULL,
    apns_topic              TEXT NOT NULL,
    push_handle             TEXT,
    created_at              TEXT NOT NULL,
    updated_at              TEXT NOT NULL
) WITHOUT ROWID;

Now the send module. There's one decision here I want your call on before I fix the contract:

questions.question: When POST /v1/notifications/register arrives, should the handler wait for the relay to mint a push handle, or store the row and register with the relay in the background?

options.label: Background, always 200 (Recommended)
options.description: Store the row with push_handle = NULL, enqueue the relay registration to the worker, return 200 immediately. Onboarding never blocks on relay availability, and the response carries a `pending` status so the app can show honest state. Downside: the app can't distinguish 'relay registration succeeded' from 'silently never happened' without a follow-up read.

options.label: Synchronous, fail if the relay is down
options.description: Call the relay inline; return 503 if it refuses or is unreachable, so the app learns immediately that notifications aren't working. Downside: couples the wallet's onboarding completion to a third-party relay's uptime, and this is the first post-promotion call the app makes.

options.label: Background, plus a status field on GET sender-keys
options.description: Background registration as above, but the sender-keys re-pin surface (which the app fetches on every Custos contact anyway) also reports whether this device's handle is live. Costs a little scope now, gives the wallet phase a real diagnostic instead of silence.

questions.question: When a payload is too large to fit the top padding bucket (3584 bytes), what should notify_device do?

options.label: Drop it and log an error (Recommended)
options.description: Refuse to send. Sending it unpadded would leak the exact length the padding exists to hide, and truncating the body would deliver a misleading notification. A dropped banner is the safe failure; the app reconciles from Custos anyway.

options.label: Truncate the body to fit
options.description: Shorten title/body until it fits a bucket. Delivers something rather than nothing, but a truncated security notice is arguably worse than no notice, and the truncation point becomes attacker-influenceable.

options.label: Send unpadded
options.description: Deliver at its natural length, accepting the metadata leak for oversized payloads only. Simplest, but it means an attacker who can influence payload size can opt a notification out of padding.

The notification relay can now actually deliver. It signs in to Apple with the operator's own push key, wraps each instance's sealed payload in the envelope Apple requires, and forwards it — carrying a fixed, content-free "Encrypted notification" placeholder that the real notification replaces once your device decrypts it. Everything that identifies the notification stays sealed: the relay copies the ciphertext through without reading it, and the only secret it holds is its own Apple credential. Two things travel back. Pushes are budgeted twice over — per instance, and per device at 60 an hour — so a bug in one instance cannot flood a phone, and one device's traffic cannot starve another's. A relay with no Apple key configured still enrolls instances and hands out push handles; it just says plainly that it cannot deliver yet. Nothing sends notifications through this yet — the Custos side that triggers them arrives next.

# Batch PR Review-Comment Triage

Pull every unresolved review thread on the current PR in one command, then triage the batch. The user should never have to paste review comments one at a time.

Determine the PR number for the current branch (`gh pr view --json number -q .number`), then:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
query($owner:String!,$repo:String!,$pr:Int!){
  repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){
    pullRequest(number:$pr){
      reviewThreads(first:100){
        nodes{
          isResolved isOutdated path line

        }
      }
    }
  }
}' -F owner=<owner> -F repo=<repo> -F pr=<number> \
| jq '[.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[]
       | select(.isResolved==false)
       | {path, line, isOutdated,
          comments: [.comments.nodes[] | {author: .author.login, url, body}]}]'
```

Also fetch top-level (non-thread) review bodies and issue comments if the bot posts summaries there:

```bash
gh pr view <number> --json reviews,comments
```

## Triage the batch

For each unresolved thread, classify before fixing anything:

1. **Correctness / security / portability** — verify the claim against the actual code, then fix if real. Automated reviewers assert confidently and are sometimes wrong; refute with evidence when they are.
2. **Legitimate but out of scope** — file a follow-up issue rather than growing the PR.
3. **Pure style nit / preference** — decline with a one-line reason.

Present the full disposition table (thread → classification → action) to the user in ONE message before applying fixes, so they approve the batch rather than each item. Note that every fix-commit re-triggers CI and (for assertive bots like CodeRabbit) a fresh review round that tends to find one more micro-nit — batch fixes into a single commit where possible.

## Resolving threads

After pushing fixes, reply/resolve via:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='mutation($id:ID!){resolveReviewThread(input:{threadId:$id}){thread{isResolved}}}' -F id=<threadId>
```

input.title: Notify: expose the send worker's queue depth as a metric
input.description:
Follow-up from review on [PR #467](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/467) (MM-418).

The notification send worker (`crates/pds/src/notify_relay_client.rs`) drains an **unbounded** `tokio::sync::mpsc` with a single sequential task. That is the right trade-off for a best-effort, device-count-scaled feature — the queue must never block a request path, and a missed push is a missed banner rather than lost data.

But during a prolonged relay outage (a maintenance window, a misconfigured node id), the queue grows without bound in the interim, and today that is only inferable from `warn!` log volume.

## Scope

Expose the current queue depth as an OTel gauge, following the existing pattern in `crates/pds/src/metrics.rs`:

* add the instrument + its name constant to `metrics::names`
* record depth from the worker (send side increments, `recv` decrements — or sample `len()` if the channel type allows)
* add the row to the metrics table in `crates/pds/AGENTS.md` (that table mirrors `metrics::names` and they change together)
* consider surfacing it in `GET /v1/admin/health` alongside the sweep entries, so the Brass Console can show it

## Why not in the original PR

Out of scope for the sender phase, and it touches the metrics module, its name constants, and the operator docs table — a self-contained change that reviews better on its own.

## Open question

Whether an unbounded queue should stay unbounded once this is observable, or gain a cap that drops oldest-first. Dropping is consistent with the feature's best-effort posture; the metric is the prerequisite for deciding with evidence either way.

All 11 threads addressed and resolved; pushed as [d0bd46ed](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/467). CI is running.

## What I fixed (9 of 11)

**Three were real bugs**, and I'd call the middle one the most valuable catch of the batch:

- **Sender scalars escaped `Zeroizing`.** `generate_sender_key` copied out of the crypto crate's wipe-on-drop buffer into a bare `[u8; 32]`, which then moved through the fan-out and was dropped unwiped — on every send. That crate keeps key material in `Zeroizing` deliberately and my unwrap boundary silently undid it.
- **A configured instance with no master key answered `200 {"keys": []}`.** A client would pin an empty set, then fail to verify every notification it received, with only a server-side warning to explain it. Now a 503 — distinct from the 501 an un-opted-in instance returns, because the operator *has* opted in.
- **The admin revoke cleanup collapsed `Err` into "no handle" and deleted the row anyway**, destroying the only record of the handle. The relay kept a live route to a just-revoked device with nothing left for a retry to find.

Plus the CLI reporting bug: `retire`/`revoke` ran guarded UPDATEs and printed success regardless, so a mistyped `kid` read as a completed revocation while the real key stayed published. That one matters because an operator revoking a key believes they've just closed a compromise.

The rest were stale comments and docs — including the `notify-relay` dependency comment claiming "only `protocol` is exposed", which stopped being true the moment I made the relay a full library. That's mine, and it's exactly the kind of drift worth catching.

## What I declined

**The `push_handle IS NULL` guard.** There's one worker draining a FIFO mpsc, awaiting each job to completion, so handle writes land in registration order and the last is by construction newest. The proposed guard would *introduce* the bug: on two back-to-back re-registrations, job 2's write gets rejected because job 1's handle is already stored — stranding the handle for the superseded APNs token. I added a comment marking the FIFO ordering as load-bearing and replied on the thread with the reasoning.

I also kept the e2e's one-byte padding tolerance while taking the raw-bytes half of that suggestion. Base64's 4-chars-per-3-bytes step makes some bucket targets unreachable by any pad length; `plaintext_pad_len` documents and tests that. Removing the allowance would assert something the arithmetic never promised.

The queue-depth gauge is deferred to [MM-487](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-487/notify-expose-the-send-workers-queue-depth-as-a-metric) — legitimate, but it touches the metrics module, its name constants, and the operator docs table, and it carries a follow-on question about whether the queue should stay unbounded once observable.

Tests are up to 2264 (from 2261): the idempotency test now covers the revoke half it was named for, plus unknown-kid no-transition, admin-handle readability after revocation, and the new 503. Full workspace clippy `-D warnings`, tests, fmt, bruno and docs parity all green locally.

One caveat on CI: **CodeRabbit is running a fresh review round** on this commit and assertive bots reliably surface a new micro-nit after each fix batch. If it does, say the word and I'll triage the next round the same way rather than reflexively applying it.
